subtype: Regular movement during a low patch [Actor]
passage: Counselling notes, Thursday. Jomon came in for his third session looking less grey around the eyes. Two weeks ago he told me he had stopped going to lectures and felt "flat, like a phone on two percent". He had tried a plan of running five kilometres every morning, gave up on day two, and called himself useless. I suggested something much smaller: a ten-minute walk to the tea stall behind the library, every day, no targets. Today he said he has missed only one day. He still feels low most evenings, but says his head is clearer before the afternoon lab, and he laughed while describing a stray dog that now waits for him at the gate. When he mentioned adding push-ups as punishment for any skipped day, I asked him to keep the walk kind instead. Next session in two weeks. Joseph, student counsellor

qa.q: Where does Jomon walk each day?
qa.a: He walks for about ten minutes to the tea stall behind the library.

qa.q: How was Jomon feeling about himself after the running plan fell apart, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and discouraged; he gave up on day two and called himself useless.

qa.q: What could Jomon try if he wants a little more movement without losing the habit?
qa.a: He could keep the daily walk as the base and add something he enjoys, like walking with a friend, only on days he feels up to it.

qa.q: How might the counsellor see Jomon's idea of push-ups as punishment?
qa.a: The counsellor sees it as turning a helpful habit back into a test Jomon can fail, so they steer him to keep the walk gentle.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a low patch finding that a short daily walk lifts energy and thinking a little, and working best as a kind habit rather than a punishment.

subtype: Overtraining and using exercise to escape [Actor]
passage:
Dolma: gym's shut for a water leak today. I'm actually shaking
Kalyani: shaking?? are you ok
Dolma: I haven't missed a day in 41 days. Two sessions most days. If I skip, it feels like the whole week is ruined
Kalyani: you also skipped my birthday dinner for the evening session
Dolma: I know. I felt awful about that
Kalyani: can I ask something without you getting mad
Dolma: go
Kalyani: does it still feel good? or does it feel like you're paying something off
Dolma: ...paying off. Every time I feel guilty about work or hate how I look, I add another hour
Kalyani: that sounds heavy. Would you talk to someone? The counsellor at your office, or a doctor?
Dolma: maybe. I'll book the counsellor tomorrow at lunch
Kalyani: I'll walk with you after, if you like. Just a slow walk, no counting 🤍

qa.q: How many days in a row has Dolma not missed exercise?
qa.a: Dolma has not missed a day in 41 days.

qa.q: Why is Dolma shaking on the day the gym is shut?
qa.a: Dolma feels anxious and guilty without a session, because exercise has become a way to pay off guilt about work and looks.

qa.q: What could help Dolma make exercise serve life again instead of ruling it?
qa.a: Honest reflection with the office counsellor or a doctor, and keeping some movement just for enjoyment, like the slow walk Kalyani offers.

qa.q: What is it like for Kalyani when Dolma picks the evening session over the birthday dinner?
qa.a: Kalyani probably felt hurt and left out, and now worries that the workouts are taking over Dolma's life.

grounding: Illustrates a person exercising compulsively to cope with guilt and body worries who feels worse on a missed day, and a friend pointing toward honest reflection and professional advice.

passage:
Coach's note, community badminton club, end of March.
Swati joined in January wanting to "get fit in one month". She came five evenings a week, played until her calves cramped, then vanished for twelve days. When she returned, red in the face, we sat on the bench and I asked what she actually liked. "Doubles. Laughing. Not the drills." So we built something smaller: Tuesday and Saturday doubles, a ten-minute stretch at home on Thursday, and Sunday fully off, written on her calendar as "rest counts too". She grumbled that rest felt like cheating. Eight weeks later she has not missed a single Tuesday, she jokes with her partners between games, and she told me she no longer dreads the Sunday guilt. I will check in with her again before the summer league starts. Rajni

qa.q: Which days does Swati play doubles now?
qa.a: She plays doubles on Tuesday and Saturday.

qa.q: Why did Swati vanish for twelve days after her first weeks?
qa.a: She was probably embarrassed after overdoing it until her calves cramped, so staying away felt easier than facing the club.

qa.q: Which choice made the new routine last, and why?
qa.a: Building it around doubles, which Swati enjoys, at a realistic two evenings a week with a planned day off; enjoyment keeps her coming back.

qa.q: How does the coach see Swati's grumble that rest felt like cheating?
qa.a: The coach reads it as all-or-nothing thinking and keeps rest written into the plan, trusting that steady play will prove it works.

grounding: Shows a young professional replacing heroic bursts with enjoyable, realistic play and planned rest days, and the steadier mood that follows.

passage: Every morning in their Pune flat, Ujjwal, her papa, takes Vasudha down to the colony park before breakfast. She squats by the ants, chases pigeons, then comes home hungry for idli. After lunch she drags her pillow to Papa by herself and curls up. On Sunday visitors came and her nap was skipped. By evening she kicked, cried at bath time and fought her pyjamas. On Monday the old rhythm returned, and she settled at night without a fuss.

qa.q: Where does Ujjwal take Vasudha every morning?
qa.a: He takes her down to the colony park before breakfast.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel on Sunday evening after missing her nap, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt cranky and overwhelmed; she kicked, cried at bath time and fought her pyjamas.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do on a day when visitors are coming?
qa.a: He could keep the park time and let Vasudha nap in a quiet room, so the day still feels familiar to her.

qa.q: What would change for Ujjwal if Vasudha had no set park, meal and nap times?
qa.a: He would probably face more fights at bath time and bedtime, since she would have fewer familiar steps to feel safe with.

grounding: Shows how regular outdoor time, meals and naps keep a toddler calm and sleeping well, and how a broken routine brings struggles at transitions.

subtype: Child cooped indoors on rainy days [Observer]
passage: By the fourth day of rain, Neelam noticed that her son Imran was shouting instead of talking and had pushed his cousin twice over one toy car. That afternoon she took him to the society's community hall, where the caretaker had laid out mats. Imran jumped, crawled through a tunnel of chairs and raced the other children to the wall and back. On the way home, Neelam let him splash through the drizzle in his raincoat. That night he sat on the window seat beside her, watching the lamps, quiet and yawning.

qa.q: What did Imran do in the community hall?
qa.a: He jumped, crawled through a tunnel of chairs and raced the other children to the wall and back.

qa.q: What might Neelam have been worried about by the fourth day of rain?
qa.a: She was likely worried and frustrated that Imran was shouting and pushing his cousin, and wondered what was making him so restless.

qa.q: How did the afternoon help, and what else could a parent try on a rainy day?
qa.a: Running and jumping let Imran use up his energy; a parent could also set up active games at home or sit with him by a bright window.

qa.q: How might Imran's cousin have felt during those rainy days?
qa.a: The cousin was probably upset and annoyed at being pushed twice over a toy car.

grounding: Shows a parent noticing a child kept indoors for days becoming loud and quarrelsome, and active play, a drizzle walk and a window seat easing his mood.

passage: Damini, sit, let me tell you about my own summer when I was ten. I'm your Vinita Masi, and I was the worst holiday sleeper in our lane. We had one TV and no rules that year. I watched films till midnight, woke at eleven, ate lunch at four. By the second week I was snapping at your mother for breathing too loudly. Then, the night before school, my stomach twisted and I cried that I would never go back. Your Nani didn't scold. The next summer she kept just two things fixed: up by seven, and cricket in the lane every evening. Everything else could float. That June, going back felt ordinary. So, Damini, what time will you wake up tomorrow?

qa.q: What two things did Nani keep fixed the next summer?
qa.a: Waking up by seven, and cricket in the lane every evening.

qa.q: What was young Vinita feeling the night before school, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt dread and fear about going back; her stomach twisted and she cried that she would never return.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Vinita's next holiday go better?
qa.a: Nani chose two simple anchors, a wake-up time and evening cricket, instead of scolding, so the return to school felt ordinary.

qa.q: How might Damini's mother have felt when young Vinita snapped at her that summer?
qa.a: She was probably hurt and annoyed, being snapped at over something as small as breathing loudly.

grounding: Illustrates a child whose holiday of late nights, TV and no fixed times leaves her grumpy and dreading school, and simple anchors smoothing the next return.

subtype: Teen living in a dim room [Actor]
passage:
Kept for Gopika's doctor visit next week. Neelam, her mother.
Since exams ended, Gopika has kept her curtains shut. I have found her at two in the afternoon under the blanket with the phone glowing, saying she "can't tell if it's Tuesday or Friday". She stopped coming out for dinner and snapped when I switched on the tube light. I didn't pull the curtains open myself. On Saturday I asked if we could try one thing together: up at eight, tea on the balcony in the morning sun, even for ten minutes. She agreed, sulking. It is day five now. She comes out on her own carrying two cups, and yesterday she laughed at the pigeons. She still looks low some evenings, so we will mention it to the doctor.

qa.q: Where do Gopika and her mother have tea in the morning?
qa.a: They have tea on the balcony in the morning sun.

qa.q: What does Gopika's remark about not knowing the day suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels lost and low, as if her days have blurred together in the dark room.

qa.q: What did Neelam's approach get right, and what is the sensible next step?
qa.a: She offered a shared morning routine instead of forcing the curtains open, and she plans to mention the low evenings to the doctor.

qa.q: How is Neelam affected when Gopika snaps about the light?
qa.a: Neelam is hurt and worried, but chooses patience over a fight, which keeps Gopika willing to try.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose mood drops in a dim room with days blurring, and morning light with a set wake-up time slowly lifting her energy.

passage: Beatriz's first month in Rotterdam was a blur of new streets, a shared kitchen that smelled of other people's dinners, and lectures in a second language. She slept at three, woke at noon and felt jittery by evening. In October she wrote four lines on a sticky note above her desk: up at 7:30. Walk along the canal. Lunch at one, dinner at seven. Saturday football. The canal walk was cold and grey, but her head felt clearer after it. On Saturdays Chidi, a midfielder from her floor, started saving her a seat on the tram. By November the city was still strange, but her days had a shape, and she caught herself humming while chopping onions.

qa.q: What did Beatriz write on the sticky note above her desk?
qa.a: Up at 7:30, a walk along the canal, lunch at one and dinner at seven, and Saturday football.

qa.q: How was Beatriz feeling in her first month, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt unsettled and jittery; she slept at three, woke at noon and was on edge by evening.

qa.q: Why did these small anchors help when everything else was new?
qa.a: They gave her days a predictable shape with regular daylight, meals and company, which steadied her mood.

qa.q: What might Chidi notice about Beatriz on Saturdays by November?
qa.a: Chidi would probably see a steadier, friendlier teammate who turns up on time, and might enjoy the regular company too.

grounding: Shows a young adult living away from home steadying her mood with a regular wake time, a morning walk, set meal times and one fixed social activity.

passage:
"You've had the lamp on since breakfast," Rafiq said, dropping his bag.
"It's four o'clock and it looks like midnight. I hate December here."
"Last December you said the same thing. And in April you were planning picnics."
Maria pulled the blanket higher. "So I'm just a sunny-weather person?"
"Maybe your body notices the dark. You've stopped your lunch walk, you sleep till nine..."
"Because it's grey and freezing."
"Tomorrow at one, when the sky's brightest, I'll come with you. Twenty minutes round the lake."
"And if I still feel like this in a month?"
"Then we book the doctor. Feeling this heavy for weeks is worth asking about."
She was quiet for a while. "Okay. One o'clock. Bring the good gloves."

qa.q: What time does Rafiq offer to walk with Maria?
qa.a: At one o'clock, when the sky is brightest, for twenty minutes round the lake.

qa.q: What does Maria's pulling the blanket higher suggest about her mood?
qa.a: She feels low and a bit defensive, stung by the idea that her mood depends on the weather.

qa.q: What sensible steps does the conversation settle on?
qa.a: Getting out at the brightest time of day, restarting the lunch walk, and seeing a doctor if the heavy mood lasts.

qa.q: How does Rafiq see Maria's December mood?
qa.a: Rafiq sees a pattern rather than a flaw, since he remembers the same dip last December and her brighter spirits in April.

grounding: Illustrates a person whose energy and mood dip in the dark months, with getting outside, keeping routines and seeing a doctor if the low lasts as sensible steps.

subtopic: Nutrition and mood in general terms
passage: In their village house near Bardhaman, Arnab pushed the bowl of shukto away. "Too slimy!" Last week his father, Vikas, had begged, then promised a toffee, and the meal had ended in tears on both sides. Tonight Vikas simply put a spoonful of the bitter-gourd dish at the edge of Arnab's plate, beside the rice and fish he liked, and talked about the goat that had escaped the neighbour's yard. Arnab ignored the spoonful. On Friday he poked it. On Sunday he tasted one piece, made a face and went back to his rice.

qa.q: What did Vikas promise last week to get Arnab to eat?
qa.a: He promised a toffee.

qa.q: Why might Arnab have pushed the bowl away?
qa.a: He felt put off and a bit stubborn, disliking the slimy texture and wanting to decide for himself.

qa.q: Which approach worked better, and why?
qa.a: Calmly placing a small spoonful beside foods Arnab liked, without fuss, because it took the fight out of the meal.

qa.q: How might meals feel for Vikas now compared with last week?
qa.a: They probably feel calmer and less draining for him, since he no longer has to beg or bargain.

grounding: Shows a young child refusing food over texture and independence, where pressure and bribes caused conflict and calm repeated offering slowly widened his taste.
